Q: How can eval() get the number of escape characters? A:

Escape characters exist to let you express characters which would otherwise mean something else in context. For example, in Python source code, many characters have special meanings, right? Like:

foo = "bar"

In this short piece of code, the " clearly have a special meaning of delimiting a string literal. The contents of the string are just bar, but to write it in code, you need to put it in quotes. foo = bar would have a different meaning.

To use quotes inside such a string literal though, what do you do?

foo = "bar "baz" quux"

This clearly doesn't work, as the meaning of the quotes conflicts here. To express the string bar "baz" quux, you need to escape the literal quotes:

foo = "bar \"baz\" quux"

Now, this is only relevant in Python source code. If you have a text file with that content, that text file is not interpreted according to Python source code syntax rules. So in a text file like this:

"bar \"baz\" quux"

This means exactly what you see. Those are 18 characters; four quotes, two backslashes, two spaces, and an assortment of letters. If you use with open(...) to read the contents of this file, you'll get exactly this text. But in Python source code, that same text has a different meaning:

>>> len("bar \"baz\" quux")
14
>>> print("bar \"baz\" quux")
bar "baz" quux

In Python code, those are only 14 characters: two quotes, two spaces, and some letters. The backslashes and the surrounding quotes are not part of the text itself, they just help express the text inside Python code.

That's the difference you need to understand, and the reason your strings behave differently depending on where they come from.

eval now takes a piece of text and evaluates it according to Python syntax rules, as if you had placed it in Python source code. So you can read text from a text file, and get the same result as if you had placed it in a Python source code file to begin with.

Q: Removing $null or Blanks from CSV Results A:

Specifically to your question; you might use the Where-Object cmdlet for this, where the following types evaluate to $false:

  • Empty strings like '' or ""
  • Null values like $null
  • Any numeric type with the value of 0

Meaning:

$TestCsv | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Test1 | Where-Object { $_ }
100
101

As an important aside: try to avoid using the <verb>-Variable cmdlets for dynamic variable names. Imaging what is going to happen when any of the column headers is called something like TESTCSV, Header or Values... 🥴
Instead, use an (ordered) HashTable (See also: How do I automatically create and use variable names?).

For your script this means:

$Column = [Ordered]@{}
foreach ($Header in $TestCsv[0].PSObject.Properties.Name) {
  $Column[$Header] =
    $TestCsv | Select-Object -ExpandProperty $Header | Where-Object { $_ }
}

Using (displaying) a specific dynamic HashTable variable (column):

$Column['Test2'] # or (using the dot-notation): $Column.Test2
200
202

To display all the HashTable (column) values:

foreach ($Header in $Column.Keys) {
  Write-Host -ForegroundColor Cyan $Header is $Column[$Header]
}
TEST1 is 100 101
TEST2 is 200 202
TEST3 is 300 303
TEST4 is 400 404

Note that in case you need to use quotes for the output string, the HashTable variable needs to be placed in a sub-expression, like: "$Header is $($Column[$Header])"

Q: Fast Live Plotting in Matplotlib / PyPlot A:

If you’re open to using a plotting library that’s built for high-FPS real-time rendering, you can avoid the whole “what’s the fastest redraw_figure()?” problem because LightningChart Python renders in a GPU-accelerated WebGL view and updates as you push new data (no explicit redraw/flush calls needed).

About LightningChart Python performance

Below is a rough equivalent of the “image + line” live update loop using a 2-row dashboard (heatmap on top, line on bottom). Heatmap updates use add_intensity_values(...) style APIs that accept efficient flat arrays / NumPy arrays.

Docs:

  • https://lightningchart.com/python-charts/docs/features/chart-xy/heatmap/

  • https://lightningchart.com/python-charts/docs/features/chart-xy/line/

  • https://lightningchart.com/python-charts/docs/guides/real-time-data/

The charts are opened in live mode (open(live=True)), so updates appear immediately.

import time
import math
import numpy as np
import lightningchart as lc

lc.set_license("my-license-key")

# 2 rows, 1 column dashboard (heatmap + line), similar to matplotlib subplots
dashboard = lc.Dashboard(columns=1, rows=2, theme=lc.Themes.Dark)

chart_hm = dashboard.ChartXY(column_index=0, row_index=0)
chart_ln = dashboard.ChartXY(column_index=0, row_index=1)

# Configure scrolling axis for spectrogram-style view
x_axis = chart_hm.get_default_x_axis()
x_axis.set_scroll_strategy(progressive=True)
x_axis.set_interval(start=-100, end=0, stop_axis_after=False)

ROWS = 100  # "frequency" resolution per column
hm = chart_hm.add_heatmap_scrolling_grid_series(
    resolution=ROWS,
    scroll_dimension="columns",
)
hm.set_start(0, 0)
hm.set_step(1, 1)
hm.hide_wireframe()
hm.enable_data_cleaning(True)

hm.set_palette_coloring(
    steps=[
        {"color": (0, 0, 120), "value": -60},
        {"color": (0, 200, 255), "value": 0},
        {"color": (255, 180, 0), "value": 40},
        {"color": (255, 0, 0), "value": 80},
    ],
    look_up_property="value",
    percentage_values=False,
)

# Line (progressive X for efficient streaming)
line = chart_ln.add_line_series(
    schema={
        "x": {"pattern": "progressive"},
        "y": {"pattern": None},
    }
)

dashboard.open(live=True)

t0 = time.time()
frames = 0

while True:
    # Heatmap update: append one new column of data for scrolling
    column = [
        40 * math.sin(idx / 12 + frames * 0.05)
        + 20 * math.cos(frames / 18)
        + np.random.randn() * 10
        for idx in range(ROWS)
    ]
    hm.add_intensity_values([column])

    # Line update (replace a small window)
    x = list(range(50))
    y = np.random.randn(50).tolist()
    line.clear()
    line.append_samples(x_values=x, y_values=y)

    frames += 1
    if frames % 60 == 0:
        fps = frames / (time.time() - t0)
        print(f"FPS: {fps:.1f}")

    # Remove if you want it to run as fast as possible
    time.sleep(0.01)

Q: Grouping with a condition A:

See example.

Group should have null and 'text' at least once

select word
from tableName
group by word
having sum(case when status is null then 1 else 0 end)>0
and sum(case when status='text' then 1 else 0 end)>0

Or, null and 'text' should appear exact once

select word
from tableName
group by word
having sum(case when status is null then 1 else 0 end)=1
and sum(case when status='text' then 1 else 0 end)=1

Or, null and 'text' should appear exact once, and nothing else.

select word
from tableName
group by word
having sum(case when status is null then 1 else 0 end)=1
and sum(case when status='text' then 1 else 0 end)=1
and count(*)=2
